q-cz-grammar.label: A blank the grammar decides
q-cz-grammar.summary: A preposition, article, conjunction or verb form that the sentence around it forces.

q-cz-sense.label: A blank the meaning decides
q-cz-sense.summary: Four possible words; the sense of the paragraph picks one.

rules.text: Read the whole paragraph once before filling anything. A cloze is one connected piece of writing, so a later sentence often settles an earlier blank.
rules.ok: Reading on shows the paragraph is about a past event, which fixes every verb tense in it.
rules.bad: Filling blank 1 from blank 1's sentence alone.

rules.text: Settle the grammar blanks first: a blank after a preposition takes a noun or an -ing form, a blank between two clauses takes a conjunction, and every verb must match the tense the paragraph has already set.
rules.ok: He succeeded in winning the seat.
rules.bad: He succeeded in win the seat.

rules.text: For a meaning blank, decide first whether the sentence is going the same way as the one before it or turning against it. A contrast word (but, however, yet) means the blank must reverse the earlier idea.
rules.ok: The scheme was generous; in practice, however, it reached very few.
rules.bad: The scheme was generous; in practice, however, it reached many.

rules.text: Put each option back in and read the whole sentence aloud. Keep the one that fits both the meaning and the words it has to combine with, since many English words take only one partner (take a decision, make a mistake, pay attention).

q-cz-grammar.cue: A paragraph with numbered blanks; the options for this blank are prepositions, articles, conjunctions or verb forms.
q-cz-grammar.standard: Read the paragraph through once. Fix the tense the paragraph is in, then fill the blank with the form the sentence around it forces.
q-cz-grammar.fast: Look only at the two or three words on each side of the blank: they usually decide a grammar blank by themselves.
q-cz-grammar.eliminate: Cross out the options whose form cannot stand in that slot at all, then choose between what is left.
traps: Filling blanks in order instead of doing the easy ones first.
Ignoring the tense the rest of the paragraph has set.
A preposition that fits the single sentence but not the fixed phrase the writer is using.

q-cz-sense.cue: A paragraph with numbered blanks; the options for this blank are four different words of the same part of speech.
q-cz-sense.standard: Decide from the sentence before whether the idea continues or turns, then pick the word that carries that direction and takes the right partner words.
q-cz-sense.fast: Find the connector (but, so, because, however) nearest the blank; it tells you which way the meaning runs.
q-cz-sense.eliminate: Drop words whose tone is wrong for the paragraph, then drop any that do not combine with the noun or verb beside them.
traps: Two options with nearly the same meaning: one of them will not fit the words around it.
Choosing the hardest-looking word instead of the one that fits.

pyqs.text:
In the paragraph below, select the most appropriate option for blank 1.

Long before electric beacons made the work largely automatic, a lighthouse keeper's life was a test of endurance against an [[___]] coastline, where a single storm could strip away a jetty overnight. The bond between the keeper and the ships that passed was quietly (2): sailors trusted the beam to find safe water, and in turn every vessel that passed word ashore so that help could be sent if the light ever failed to appear. The coast offered little mercy to the (3) traveller who misjudged the tide, and more than one rescue began only because a keeper's lamp had been left burning through a night when no ship was expected. For the families who grew up in these towers, the sound of the foghorn left an (4) impression, one that no later, quieter life could ever fully erase. Even today, as satellite navigation has made the manned lighthouse all but obsolete, the keeper's solitary vigil still carries a strange (5) for anyone who has ever waited, alone, for a signal that might not come.
pyqs.why: A coastline that can 'strip away a jetty overnight' gives no comfort or shelter, so it is 'inhospitable', harsh and unwelcoming.

a.note: 'Hospitable' is the direct opposite of the harsh coast the sentence goes on to describe.

b.note: 'Tranquil' says the coast is calm, but the sentence is about its power to destroy a jetty.

d.note: 'Fertile' describes land good for growing things, not a dangerous coastline.

In the paragraph below, select the most appropriate option for blank 2.

Long before electric beacons made the work largely automatic, a lighthouse keeper's life was a test of endurance against an (1) coastline, where a single storm could strip away a jetty overnight. The bond between the keeper and the ships that passed was quietly [[___]]: sailors trusted the beam to find safe water, and in turn every vessel that passed word ashore so that help could be sent if the light ever failed to appear. The coast offered little mercy to the (3) traveller who misjudged the tide, and more than one rescue began only because a keeper's lamp had been left burning through a night when no ship was expected. For the families who grew up in these towers, the sound of the foghorn left an (4) impression, one that no later, quieter life could ever fully erase. Even today, as satellite navigation has made the manned lighthouse all but obsolete, the keeper's solitary vigil still carries a strange (5) for anyone who has ever waited, alone, for a signal that might not come.
pyqs.why: The sentence describes a two-way exchange — sailors trust the beam, and ships send word back — so the bond is 'reciprocal', given and returned by both sides.

a.note: 'Unilateral' means coming from one side only, which contradicts the 'and in turn' that follows.

c.note: 'One-sided' again denies the two-way exchange the sentence describes.

d.note: 'Accidental' says the bond happened by chance, not that it was returned on both sides.

In the paragraph below, select the most appropriate option for blank 5.

Even today, as satellite navigation has made the manned lighthouse all but obsolete, the keeper's solitary vigil still carries a strange [[___]] for anyone who has ever waited, alone, for a signal that might not come.
pyqs.why: Even though the lighthouse itself is 'all but obsolete', the image of a solitary vigil still strikes an emotional chord with the reader, which is its 'resonance', the lingering power to move someone.

b.note: 'Irrelevance' says the image no longer matters, the opposite of 'still carries' something.

c.note: 'Obsolescence' repeats the earlier point about the lighthouse being outdated, not the feeling it still provokes.

d.note: 'Ambiguity' means being unclear in meaning, not striking an emotional chord.

pyqs.text:
In the paragraph below, select the most appropriate option for blank 1.

After thirty years on the bench, Judge Ortiz had grown accustomed to the small rituals of a trial: the opening statements, the parade of exhibits, the occasional objection raised more as a [[___]] than as a serious challenge to the evidence. What she found harder to grow accustomed to was the way a jury's first impression of a witness, once formed, tended to resist every later correction. A witness who seemed (2) with the facts already established would be believed almost without question, while one whose account, however accurate, failed to fit the story the jury had already assembled in its mind would struggle to be heard at all. Jurors did not set out to be unfair; they simply became (3) to detail that did not confirm what they had decided early on. The judge had come to doubt whether even an entirely (4) slip, a wrong date, a misremembered colour, ever read as harmless once suspicion had taken hold. What she still believed, after all those years, was that a patient, (5) witness, one who corrected their own small errors rather than cover them, usually won a jury over in the end, however long it took.
pyqs.why: An objection raised without being a serious challenge is a 'cavil', a trivial or petty objection, matching 'more as a ... than as a serious challenge'.

a.note: 'Exculpation' means clearing someone of blame, unrelated to raising an objection.

c.note: 'Imputation' means an accusation or suggestion of wrongdoing, not a trivial objection to evidence.

d.note: 'Salience' means being prominent or noticeable, which does not fit 'objection' at all.

pyqs.text:
In the paragraph below, select the most appropriate option for blank 1.

An arbitral tribunal, entrusted with resolving commercial disputes outside the ordinary courts, draws its authority not from any claim to coercive power but from the confidence of the parties who submit to its award. Where a tribunal's reasoning is transparent and its procedure evenly applied, an award commands voluntary compliance; where it is not, the promise of a binding decision risks becoming a [[___]] formality, honoured in name but ignored in practice. At the same time, a tribunal must resist the temptation to expand its own brief, lest its members (2) powers of review that the parties never conferred on them and that properly belong to a court of appeal. This tension between deference and vigilance is compounded by a further difficulty: the sheer (3) with which many tribunals move from filing to final award, a slowness that leaves commercial relationships in limbo for years and erodes the very confidence the system depends on. Where delay is allowed to become routine, the appearance of fairness can (4) its substance altogether, however scrupulously the final award is reasoned.
pyqs.why: A formality that is 'honoured in name but ignored in practice' has no real force, which is exactly 'nugatory': having no practical value or effect.

b.note: 'Inviolable' means never to be broken or dishonoured, the opposite of a promise that is ignored in practice.

c.note: 'Sacrosanct' means too important to be interfered with, again the opposite of an ignored formality.

d.note: 'Immutable' means unable to be changed, which says nothing about whether the promise is honoured or ignored.

At the same time, a tribunal must resist the temptation to expand its own brief, lest its members [[___]] powers of review that the parties never conferred on them and that properly belong to a court of appeal. This tension between deference and vigilance is compounded by a further difficulty: the sheer (3) with which many tribunals move from filing to final award, a slowness that leaves commercial relationships in limbo for years and erodes the very confidence the system depends on. Where delay is allowed to become routine, the appearance of fairness can (4) its substance altogether, however scrupulously the final award is reasoned.
pyqs.why: Tribunal members taking for themselves a power of review 'that the parties never conferred on them' are seizing an authority they have no right to, which is to 'usurp' it.

b.note: 'Abrogate' means to formally repeal or do away with a law or agreement, not to seize a power for oneself.

c.note: 'Repudiate' means to reject or refuse to accept something, the opposite of seizing it.

d.note: 'Circumscribe' means to restrict within limits, not to take a power for oneself.

practice.text:
In the paragraph below, select the most appropriate option for blank 1.

For most of the last century the bicycle was treated in Indian cities as a vehicle for those who could afford [[___]] else. Road width went to cars, and the cyclist was pushed to the broken edge of the carriageway. That assumption is now being questioned, (2) because of any affection for the bicycle, but because the arithmetic of space has become impossible to ignore: a lane of cars moves a few thousand people an hour, while the same lane given to cycles moves several times as many. Cities that have (3) the change report a further gain they had not counted on. Shopkeepers on streets closed to cars at first (4) the plan, and then found their takings rising, because a cyclist stops where a driver passes by. The lesson is modest but useful: street space is not a fixed quantity to be shared out, and what a street carries (5) on how it is arranged.
practice.why: The sentence means the bicycle was for people with no other choice, so 'could afford nothing else' is the sense required.

a.note: 'Could afford anything else' reverses the meaning: it would describe people with money.

c.note: 'Something else' would mean they had another option, which contradicts 'pushed to the broken edge'.

d.note: 'Everything else' makes the sentence say they could afford all other vehicles.

practice.text:
In the paragraph below, select the most appropriate option for blank 1.

Weather forecasting improved more in the last forty years than in the four centuries before them, and almost none of that gain came from better instruments. It came from [[___]] that the atmosphere obeys equations which a large enough computer can solve step by step. The method has one unavoidable weakness. A forecast begins from a picture of today's atmosphere, and that picture is never (2); a small error in it grows as the calculation runs forward, until after about ten days the forecast says nothing at all. Forecasters live with this (3) running the same model many times from slightly different starting pictures. Where the runs agree, the forecast is firm; where they scatter, it is not, (4) a forecast is now given as a chance rather than a statement. The honest number is more useful than the confident one, (5) it is harder to put on a television screen.
practice.why: After the preposition 'from' the verb takes the -ing form: from realising that.

a.note: 'From realise' puts a base verb after a preposition.

c.note: 'From realised' puts a past form after a preposition.

d.note: 'Realisation' is a noun and would need 'of' or 'that' handled differently: 'from the realisation that'.

A forecast begins from a picture of today's atmosphere, and that picture is never [[___]]; a small error in it grows as the calculation runs forward, until after about ten days the forecast says nothing at all. Forecasters live with this (3) running the same model many times from slightly different starting pictures. Where the runs agree, the forecast is firm; where they scatter, it is not, (4) a forecast is now given as a chance rather than a statement. The honest number is more useful than the confident one, (5) it is harder to put on a television screen.
practice.why: The next clause says a small error in the picture grows, so the picture is never exactly right.

b.note: 'Never useful' contradicts the paragraph, which says the method improved forecasting greatly.

c.note: 'Never recent' makes no sense of a picture of today's atmosphere.

d.note: 'Complete' is close to the sense but the sentence is answered by 'a small error in it', which is about accuracy, not coverage.

b.note: 'For running' would give a purpose rather than the means.

c.note: 'With running' does not form the means-expressing phrase that 'by' does.

d.note: 'To running' puts a preposition where an infinitive marker cannot go.

a.note: 'Because' reverses cause and effect: the chance form follows from the scatter, not the other way round.

b.note: 'Although' makes it a contrast, but the two halves agree with each other.

The honest number is more useful than the confident one, [[___]] it is harder to put on a television screen.
practice.why: The honest number being harder to present is a drawback set against its usefulness, so the blank marks a contrast.

a.note: 'Because' would make the difficulty the reason for the usefulness, which reverses the sense.

c.note: 'So that' gives a purpose, and being hard to show on a screen is not a purpose.

d.note: 'As if' introduces a comparison, which the sentence is not making.

practice.text:
In the paragraph below, select the most appropriate option for blank 1.

Urban planners have long debated whether a city's transport network should be designed around private cars or public transit, but the clearest lesson from the last two decades is that the two cannot expand together forever: road space is [[___]], and every new lane added for cars quickly fills with more traffic than it was built to carry. Cities that have instead invested in frequent, reliable buses and trains have found that commuters switch readily once the alternative is actually (2), rather than a timetable that exists only on paper.
practice.why: Lanes added for cars 'quickly fill with more traffic than it was built to carry' only if the supply of road space cannot keep growing, so the blank needs 'finite', meaning limited in amount.

b.note: 'Abundant' says there is plenty of road space, the opposite of a space that fills up as fast as it is built.

c.note: 'Renewable' describes a resource that replenishes itself, not one that is simply limited in amount.

d.note: 'Cheap' is about cost, not about how much road space exists.

Cities that have instead invested in frequent, reliable buses and trains have found that commuters switch readily once the alternative is actually [[___]], rather than a timetable that exists only on paper.
practice.why: The contrast with 'a timetable that exists only on paper' shows the blank needs a word for something commuters can actually believe in and rely on, which is 'credible'.

b.note: 'Theoretical' repeats the very idea the sentence is contrasting against ('exists only on paper'), rather than opposing it.

c.note: 'Optional' is about choice, not about whether the service can be trusted to exist.

d.note: 'Expensive' is about cost, which the sentence never raises.
